content.title: A p99 forty times the median: tracing latency spikes to one 3 MB array
content.text:
The report-rendering service in our billing platform, called Tallyhouse, runs on the JVM with an 8 GB heap under G1. For six weeks its p99 latency sat at 1.8 seconds while p50 was 41 milliseconds and p90 was 78. A p99 forty times the median is a signature worth taking seriously, because it usually means a small fraction of requests are hitting a different code path or a different machine state, not that the whole service is slow. This is the investigation, edited down from the internal document.

We ruled out the network first: client-side and server-side latency histograms agreed to within 2 ms at every percentile, so the time was inside the process. We ruled out the database next: the p99 of query time was 34 ms, and the slow requests, when we sampled 200 of them from traces, spent a median of 29 ms in queries. We ruled out lock contention using a 60-second wall-clock profile, which showed 0.4 percent of samples in monitor-enter. What the traces did show was that the slow requests had no slow span: a request of 1.7 seconds total would have spans summing to 90 ms and 1.6 seconds of nothing. Unaccounted time inside a JVM process with no blocking span is almost always a safepoint, and the usual reason for a long safepoint is garbage collection.

The GC log confirmed it. Young collections ran every 400 ms with pauses of 8 to 15 ms, which is fine. But every 30 to 90 seconds there was a pause of 1.4 to 2.1 seconds labelled Pause Young (Concurrent Start), followed shortly by a Remark pause and a mixed collection, and the heap occupancy graph looked like a sawtooth with a cliff: it climbed to about 6.9 GB, triggered a concurrent cycle, and dropped to 2.1 GB. The interesting figure was humongous regions. G1 divides the heap into regions, 4 MB each for an 8 GB heap since it targets 2,048 regions, and any object larger than half a region, here 2 MB, is a humongous object allocated directly into contiguous old-generation regions. Our log showed 850 to 1,100 humongous regions at the start of each concurrent cycle, meaning 3.4 to 4.4 GB of the heap was humongous objects at peak.

Allocation profiling over 10 minutes attributed 71 percent of allocated bytes to one frame: a byte array of 3,145,728 bytes, exactly 3 MB, created in the PDF rendering path for every report request as a scratch buffer to hold the entire rendered document before compression. Most reports compressed to under 200 KB; the 3 MB was a hard-coded maximum chosen years earlier. At 60 requests per second, that is 180 MB per second of humongous allocation, or about 45 fresh humongous regions per second. Each one occupies a full 4 MB region even though 3 MB leaves 1 MB unused, so the effective waste was 25 percent on top of the allocation itself.

Humongous objects hurt G1 in three ways that compound. They bypass the young generation, so they are reclaimed only at the end of a concurrent cycle or, opportunistically during young collections, if they are primitive arrays with no references; ours qualified, but the eager reclamation check runs per region and the sheer count made young pauses longer too. They fragment the old generation, because a 3 MB object needs one 4 MB region and cannot share it, and when the free list has no contiguous region the collector falls back to a full compaction. And they inflate old-generation occupancy, which drove us across the 45 percent initiating heap occupancy threshold every 30 to 90 seconds, starting concurrent cycles whose initial pause included scanning roots across a heap that was mostly dead scratch buffers. The 1.4 to 2.1 second pauses were the collector working hard to discover that almost everything was garbage.

The fix was two changes. The scratch buffer became a chunked output stream that allocates 64 KB segments from a bounded pool and grows on demand, so a typical 180 KB report touches three segments and nothing crosses the humongous threshold. And we raised the G1 region size to 16 MB as a belt-and-braces measure for the remaining large allocations in the image-decoding path, which pushed the humongous threshold to 8 MB. After deployment, humongous regions at cycle start fell from about 1,000 to 12. Concurrent cycles now trigger every 14 minutes rather than every minute. p99 dropped from 1.8 seconds to 96 ms, and p50 improved from 41 to 37 ms because young pauses also shortened. Steady-state heap footprint fell by 3.1 GB, and we later reduced the heap to 5 GB with no regression.

The general lesson is that under G1 the cost of an allocation is discontinuous at half the region size. A 1.9 MB array and a 2.1 MB array on an 8 GB heap are allocated by completely different mechanisms with completely different lifecycle costs, and nothing in the source code signals the boundary. Any per-request allocation should be checked against that threshold, which you can compute from the heap size, and the humongous region count from the GC log should be on a dashboard next to pause time. We would also now treat a fixed maximum-size buffer as a smell in any hot path: it is sized for the worst case and paid for on every case.

notes: Text is the capped extract of a ~4,000-word piece; harness overrides wordCount to 4100 / readingMinutes to 18 so this exercises the save rule. A correct judge should recognise a dense, high-value JVM investigation (elimination of causes, humongous-allocation mechanism, measured fix) and recommend saving it for later given the long reading time.
